name: The Prompt Tuner
oneLiner: A/B-tests draft system prompts over a shared prompt set and scores which one makes responses shorter, more on-point, and less pushy.
lead: The same assistant reads as rambling or crisp depending on its system prompt. This agent runs one fixed prompt set through several draft system prompts, scores each on a six-dimension rubric — length, relevance, follow-up quality, tone, and more — and ranks them against a no-prompt baseline. The baseline is the starting line every draft is measured against.
chore: Tuning how an assistant talks is normally guesswork: tweak the instructions, eyeball a few replies, form a gut feeling. There's no consistent way to tell whether a new draft actually shortened responses, held relevance, cut the pushy 'would you like me to...' follow-ups, or warmed the tone — and no way to prove the change helped rather than regressed.
instead: Every draft is scored on the same rubric — word count, relevance, follow-up quality, tone, and more — against the no-prompt baseline, with a named winner and the exact per-dimension delta each draft moved.
whyItMatters: Shorter, sharper, less pushy responses are the difference between an assistant people reach for and one they find exhausting.

howItWorks.step: Parses a spreadsheet of conversation prompts into a prompt bank, carrying each row's target response size (S/M/L/XL) and whether follow-ups are none, optional, or expected.
howItWorks.explain: Row normalization is **whitelist-validated, not trusting**: `responseSize` is only accepted if `responseSizeRaw.toUpperCase()` lands in `['S','M','L','XL']`, and `followUpExpected` likewise against `['none','optional','expected']` — any junk value becomes `undefined` rather than a bad enum that would corrupt the later complexity/limit logic. The `id` falls back to a synthetic `P-${i + 1}` when no `prompt_id` column exists (or a row's cell is blank), so every prompt is addressable in the report even for an id-less sheet. Note the deliberate asymmetry in defaults: `difficulty` defaults to `'medium'` (it's needed as the fallback complexity signal downstream), but `responseSize` and `followUpExpected` stay `undefined` when unspecified — signaling 'no explicit target' so the scoring can fall back to difficulty instead of assuming a size.

howItWorks.step: The platform's system-prompt layer isn't swappable, so each draft is prepended to the user message inside labeled `[SYSTEM CONTEXT]` / `[USER MESSAGE]` markers.
howItWorks.explain: This encodes a real **platform limitation as a methodology caveat**: the assistant's true system-prompt layer isn't swappable, so the draft is *prepended* to the user turn inside explicit `[SYSTEM CONTEXT]` / `[USER MESSAGE]` markers rather than installed as a genuine system prompt. The markers matter — they give the model a structural cue to treat the draft as standing instructions instead of part of the question, the closest available approximation. The `systemPromptText ? ... : prompt.prompt` ternary is what makes the **baseline** run honest: when no draft is supplied it sends the bare prompt with *no* wrapper at all, so baseline measures true no-instruction behavior rather than an empty-context artifact. The honest framing is that this measures instruction-following under prepended context, not true system-prompt control.

howItWorks.step: Counts response words and checks them against a complexity-tiered ceiling (simple/moderate/complex), flagging ok / warn / fail.
howItWorks.explain: This is a **deterministic length gate — no LLM** — so verbosity is measured identically every run. Word count is `split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean)`, where the `filter(Boolean)` drops empty tokens from leading/multiple whitespace so padding can't inflate the count. The complexity ladder is **`responseSize`-first, `difficulty`-fallback**: an explicit `S`/`M` maps to simple/moderate, *any other* set `responseSize` (i.e. `L`/`XL`) collapses to `complex`, and only when `responseSize` is `undefined` does it read `difficulty` (easy/hard, else moderate) — honoring the per-row size target when given and degrading gracefully when not. Watch the flag boundaries carefully: `flag` is `ok` at `<= target`, else `warn` up through **`t.fail`**, else `fail` — so the `t.warn` threshold in the table is not actually consulted here; the warn band is simply everything between `target` and `fail`.

howItWorks.step: Regex-detects follow-up suggestions in the reply, classifies each as action vs. question, and counts them against a recommended limit of 3.
howItWorks.explain: This is a **deterministic detector for the 'pushy follow-up' anti-pattern**, run before the judge so its findings can be fed in as context. It scans for three canned solicitation phrasings (`would you like`, `do you want`, `want me to`), and `match(pattern) || []` guards the null that `String.match` returns on no hit so the spread doesn't throw. Dedup via `Set` then `slice(0, 10)` caps the list — a reply that spams the same nudge is collapsed to one, and the cap bounds pathological cases. Each item is typed **question vs action** by a cheap heuristic (`endsWith('?')` or an interrogative-verb prefix), letting the report distinguish a genuine offer from a templated question. The bright line is `<= 3`: `withinLimit` and the `note` both key off it, so anything beyond three recommended follow-ups is flagged as exceeding the limit.

howItWorks.step: Scores each reply with an LLM-as-judge on six dimensions — accuracy, relevance, conciseness, hallucination resistance, follow-up quality, tone — feeding the pre-computed word-count and follow-up analysis as context.
howItWorks.explain: This is the **hybrid deterministic-plus-LLM design**: rather than asking the judge to eyeball length or count nudges (which models do unreliably), the pre-computed `wordCountCheck.wordCount` and `followUpAnalysis.count` are injected into the prompt as **FOLLOW-UP CONTEXT** and **WORD COUNT CONTEXT**, grounding the model's `conciseness` and `follow_up_quality` scores in hard numbers it can't miscount. The rubrics are **explicit-breakpoint** (`follow_up_quality: '10 = none needed and none shown, ...'`) precisely to reduce inter-run judge variance — a common LLM-as-judge failure is drifting scales, and anchored breakpoints pin them. Output is parsed with the same defensive `match(/\{[^}]+\}/)` first-JSON-block extraction used elsewhere (guards a judge that wraps JSON in prose, flat objects only), then each 1-10 score is normalized to 0-1 and averaged across the six dimensions into the aggregate the ranking uses.

howItWorks.step: After a draft runs over the full prompt bank, aggregates verdict counts, per-dimension averages, and mean word/follow-up counts into one summary, ready to diff against baseline or another draft.
howItWorks.explain: This collapses one draft's whole run into a **single comparable row** keyed by `systemPromptLabel`, which is what lets a bake-off line drafts up against each other and the baseline. The `dimAvg` helper is defensively written: `.find(...)?.normalizedScore ?? 0` treats a dimension the judge omitted as **0**, so a malformed judge reply drags that dimension's mean down rather than throwing or silently skewing it upward — a conservative choice that surfaces judge failures instead of hiding them. Carrying both the `verdictCounts` histogram and the continuous `averageScores` means a comparison can be read two ways: the discrete PASS/WARNING/FAIL mix, and the fine-grained per-dimension deltas (`conciseness`, `follow_up_quality`, `conversational_tone`, plus the `aggregate`) that show *where* one draft actually moved the needle versus baseline.

examples.caption: Baseline vs. a 'be concise' draft
examples.input: 30 conversation prompts, run first with no system prompt, then with a draft instructing the assistant to keep answers short.
examples.output: The draft cut mean response length from 240 to 110 words, raised conciseness from 0.61 to 0.88, and moved the overall verdict from WARNING to PASS — a clear win over baseline.

examples.caption: Catching a pushy-follow-up regression
examples.input: A draft that makes the assistant end every reply with several 'Would you like me to explain further?' questions.
examples.output: A low follow_up_quality score with the note '5 follow-ups — exceeds recommended limit of 3, mostly templated questions,' flagging that the draft made the assistant read as scripted.

examples.caption: A three-way bake-off
examples.input: The baseline plus three draft system prompts, all run over the same 30 prompts.
examples.output: A ranked table naming draft 2 the winner on the best brevity/tone blend, plus a delta table: draft 2 beat baseline by 12 points on pass rate while draft 3 regressed below baseline.

underHood.heading: Parses the prompt bank
underHood.whenRuns: First, before any draft is tested.
underHood.output: A prompt bank carrying each prompt's target response size and follow-up expectation.

underHood.heading: Prepends the draft and queries the assistant
underHood.whenRuns: Once per prompt, per draft (and once with no prompt, for baseline).
underHood.input: One prompt, plus the draft system-prompt text (or nothing, for baseline).
underHood.output: The assistant's real reply to the combined message.

underHood.heading: Checks response length
underHood.input: The reply text and the prompt's complexity tier.
underHood.output: A word count against the tiered ceiling, flagged ok / warn / fail.

underHood.heading: Detects and classifies follow-ups
underHood.output: A follow-up count, each labeled action or question, against the limit of 3.

underHood.heading: Scores with an LLM judge
underHood.whenRuns: After the length and follow-up checks, using them as context.
underHood.input: The reply, plus the pre-computed length and follow-up analysis.
underHood.output: A 1-10 score on six dimensions: accuracy, relevance, conciseness, hallucination resistance, follow-up quality, tone.

underHood.heading: Aggregates and compares
underHood.whenRuns: Last, once a draft has run over every prompt.
underHood.input: Every scored reply for that draft.
underHood.output: One summary of per-dimension means and word/follow-up counts — set against baseline and other drafts to name a winner.

prerequisites: Node >= 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
A spreadsheet of conversation prompts — a prompt column, and ideally target-response-size and follow-up-expectation columns.
One or more draft system prompts saved as `.txt` files — the instruction variants you want to A/B-test.
The assistant API's base URL and access token.
The toolkit's local checker service running, for the privacy/safety half of the scoring.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed by Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: Needed only the first time on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone the agent code, install dependencies, and start the local checker service.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

# one-time: install the checker service's own dependencies
npm run eval:service:install

# then start it (leave this running in its own terminal tab)
npm run eval:service:start
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the xlsx reader, the report writers, and the assistant client. The checker service runs the privacy/safety half of scoring — it must be up before evaluating.
steps.firstRun: Installs everything and starts the service listening locally.
steps.rerun: Leave the service up across tuning runs — no restart per run.

steps.label: Point it at the assistant (env vars).
steps.why: Read at startup: which assistant to query and the token that authorizes it. Nothing is hard-coded — swap these to retarget environments.

steps.label: Convert the spreadsheet into a prompt bank, then measure the no-prompt baseline.
steps.cmd:
npm run opt:convert -- --input path/to/conversation-questions.xlsx
npm run opt:baseline
steps.why: `opt:convert` builds the prompt bank the run consumes. `opt:baseline` runs every prompt with no draft attached — the vanilla behavior every draft is measured against.
steps.firstRun: Parses the spreadsheet, then queries every prompt with no system prompt attached and scores each reply.
steps.rerun: Re-measure the baseline whenever the underlying assistant itself changes, so the comparison point stays honest.

steps.label: Run one draft, or bake several off against each other.
steps.cmd:
# one draft
npm run opt:run -- --system-prompt inputs/system-prompts/draft-v1.txt --sp-label v1

# several drafts, bake-off style
npm run opt:compare -- --system-prompts draft-v1.txt,draft-v2.txt
steps.why: Each draft is prepended to every prompt before sending (the platform doesn't allow swapping the real system prompt — noted in the run so results are read correctly). `opt:compare` runs several drafts back to back and ranks them.
steps.firstRun: Runs the whole prompt bank once per draft and scores every reply on six dimensions.
steps.rerun: Safe to re-run after tweaking a draft — each run gets its own labeled, timestamped report.

steps.label: Open the comparison.
steps.cmd:
open outputs/response-opt/opt-run-<label>-<timestamp>.xlsx
# a short plain-text summary anyone can paste into chat:
open outputs/response-opt/opt-run-<label>-<timestamp>-SHAREABLE.txt
steps.why: The `.xlsx` has the full per-draft breakdown — word counts, follow-up counts, and all six dimensions — against baseline. The SHAREABLE.txt is the short form for a ticket or chat.

inputs.name: --system-prompt <path>
inputs.desc: One draft system prompt (a .txt file) to test.

inputs.name: --sp-label <name>
inputs.desc: A short label for that draft, e.g. v1, v2 — shown in every report.

inputs.name: --system-prompts <a,b,c>
inputs.desc: Several draft system prompts to bake off against each other and the baseline in one run.

inputs.name: --limit <n>
inputs.desc: Run only the first N prompts — a quick check before a full run.

outputs.name: opt-run-<label>-<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: The full run for one draft — word counts, follow-up counts, and the six-dimension scores.

outputs.name: opt-run-<label>-<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: A formatted spreadsheet of the same run, color-coded by PASS / WARNING / FAIL.

outputs.name: opt-run-<label>-<timestamp>-SHAREABLE.txt
outputs.desc: A short plain-text summary for pasting anywhere.

runbook.rerun: Re-measure the baseline only when the underlying assistant changes; drafts can be re-run freely after every tweak, since each run is independent and separately labeled — nothing is overwritten.
runbook.integrate: This is how a team picks which draft system prompt ships — the ranked comparison against baseline is the evidence, not a gut feeling. Promote the winning `.txt` to the new baseline, and re-run the bake-off any time someone proposes another wording change.

video.caption: 3-4 min screencast: bake off two draft system prompts against the no-prompt baseline.
script: Open a terminal beside the two draft `.txt` files and the outputs folder so viewers see both.
Say: 'This agent measures whether a new draft of the assistant's rulebook actually makes it sound better. Watch.'
Show the two draft files side by side — one plain, one asking for shorter, warmer replies.
Run `node -v` and `npm install`; explain Node runs the agent and npm install grabs its libraries.
Start the local checker service; say it's the piece that scores privacy and safety.
Run the convert step, then the baseline run; explain the baseline is the 'no rulebook at all' starting line.
Run the compare command across both drafts; narrate the word-count and follow-up lines as they scroll by.
Open the produced `.xlsx`; scroll to the ranking table and read out the winner and its score gap over baseline.
Point at the follow-up-quality column for the losing draft and read its low-scoring note out loud.
Close: 'That winning draft's .txt file is what gets promoted to be the assistant's next rulebook.'
